new_statements.quote: Stress is predictable. In two and three syllable words stress occurs on the first syllable. In four and five syllable words primary stress occurs on the second syllable. On long verbs there are layers of stress. Vowel length is an important feature in Buin, but is not interpreted as phonemic but as sequences of single vowels. All vowels can be lengthened 2-4 times.
new_statements.citation: Griffin, Margie. 1996. Buin Organised Phonology Data (Buin (Telei, Terei) Language [BUO]). 4 pp. manuscript, SIL PNG Branch, Ukarumpa (data checked June 1996; printed 2004-08-17). SIL Language & Culture Archives entry 42446.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (4 pp., text layer, PDF metadata Author 'SIL PNG Branch', Title 'OPD', Subject 'Buin', created 2004-08-16). extracted text of page 3 contains, under the heading 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)', exactly: 'Stress is predictable. In two and three syllable words stress occurs on the first syllable. In four and five syllable words primary stress occurs on the second syllable. On long verbs there are layers of stress.' followed (after a blank line, as a separate paragraph) by 'Vowel length is an important feature in Buin, but is not interpreted as phonemic but as sequences of single vowels. All vowels can be lengthened 2-4 times.' The reported quote joins these two paragraphs but…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-contrastive and counted from the left, but its position depends on word length: initial syllable in words of two or three syllables, second syllable in words of four or five syllables; long (polysyllabic) verbs carry several stresses. Note that the same source treats long vowels as sequences of single vowels (each a syllable beat, up to four), so the syllable count that drives the rule includes each vowel beat and syllabic nasals.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Only 'On long verbs there are layers of stress'; no explicit secondary-stress rule.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Contradicted by the much older Grisward 1910 (Anthropos 5: 84), who says accent and vowel length change word meaning and gives five minimal pairs (e.g. mátsi 'grass' vs matsi 'niece'; kototsi 'I draw water' vs kotótsi 'to finish'), implying contrastive accent; Laycock 1969 and 2003 are silent on stress and do not mark it.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (isolated words by syllable count); the OPD covers the language as 'Buin (Telei, Terei) [BUO]' without specifying a dialect. A 4-page SIL data sheet posted 'as is' without peer review, but compiled by the SIL fieldworker on Buin since 1964.
new_statements.identity_note: Griffin 1996 covers the language under the heading 'Buin (Telei, Terei) Language [BUO]' with no dialect specified (SIL worked in the central Buin area). Laycock 2003 (p. xi) distinguishes Eastern, Northern, Northeastern (Uisai), Southern and Western dialects; the OPD statement should be taken as central/general Buin (tere1278), not specifically Uisai.

sources.note: p.3 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)': stress is predictable; first syllable in 2-3 syllable words, primary stress on the second syllable in 4-5 syllable words, 'layers of stress' on long verbs; vowel length not phonemic but sequences of single vowels (2-4 beats).
